analysis.one_liner: Bans all new offshore oil, gas, and mineral leasing in federal waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its subcommittee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the federal government from issuing any new lease for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in federal offshore waters [S2][S3]. It was introduced in May 2010, shortly after the BP Deepwater Horizon spill in the Gulf of Mexico [S1]. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it stayed without any hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing and tourism businesses, and people who use public beaches and waters gain protection from the risks of new offshore drilling, including spills like the one then unfolding in the Gulf. Taxpayers also avoid bearing cleanup and disaster costs that historically follow major offshore spills.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the issuance of any new lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or any other mineral on the outer Continental Shelf [S2][S3].

Introduced six days after Rep. Pallone joined the bill on May 6, 2010, in the aftermath of the BP Deepwater Horizon rig explosion and spill (April 2010), which showed how offshore disasters impose costs on coastal economies and taxpayers [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to unleased federal offshore areas for future drilling, and the nation forgoes some future domestic production, which could put modest upward pressure on energy prices and increase reliance on imports.

drawbacks.text: A permanent ban on new offshore leases would reduce future domestic oil and gas supply, which opponents would argue raises energy costs for consumers and increases dependence on foreign producers. The bill as drafted offers no phase-in or exceptions [S3].
The ban covers all minerals on the outer Continental Shelf, not just oil and gas, so it forecloses even broadly supported new energy development in federal waters without exception [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects coastal economies and waters from new drilling risk at the cost of some future domestic energy supply. The tradeoff is real: a total, permanent ban is a blunt instrument, and energy prices would be somewhat affected over time, though existing leases would have continued producing. Weighing spill risk against supply, the public-protection side is the larger effect, but the bill's absolute scope is a fair criticism.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ) introduced the bill on May 6, 2010 [S1][S2].
Seven Democratic cosponsors joined, all from the House's 253-member Democratic caucus [S4].
The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee on May 6, 2010, and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on May 10, 2010; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off because the bill died: they kept the legal pathway to new federal offshore leases, and no new restrictions on drilling in federal waters were enacted this session.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban new offshore leasing

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it was referred to a subcommittee on May 10, 2010, and died there

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored and cosponsored the bill, but no vote was ever taken, so the parties' actual positions were never tested on the record.

industries.note: The bill would cut the industry off from any new federal offshore leases, ending its pipeline of future drilling acreage. Its gain from the bill's failure is continued access to public waters, the same access that carries spill risk for coastal communities.
These businesses depend on clean waters and beaches; the bill would reduce the risk of new offshore spills that could shut down fishing grounds and tourism, as the 2010 Gulf spill demonstrated.
Rig operators and drilling services companies would lose future work as unleased federal offshore areas closed to new development.
